notes.title: Introduction to Web Publishing
notes.content: Web publishing on Unix systems typically involves using Apache or another web server to serve static files or dynamic content. Each user may have a public_html directory for hosting pages.

notes.title: CGI Basics
notes.content: The Common Gateway Interface (CGI) allows a web server to run external programs to generate dynamic web content. These programs can be written in C, Python, Perl, or shell scripts.

notes.title: CGI Workflow
notes.content:
1. Browser requests a URL.
2. Server executes the CGI script.
3. Script processes input and produces HTML.
4. Server returns HTML to the browser.

notes.title: Permissions & Security
notes.content: CGI scripts must be executable by the web server and carefully secured to avoid vulnerabilities such as code injection. Use correct shebangs, validate input, and set appropriate permissions.

flashcards.front: What does CGI stand for in web publishing?
Where do Unix users typically store web pages for publishing?
What is the role of the shebang (#!) in CGI scripts?
flashcards.back: It specifies the interpreter that should run the script (e.g., #!/usr/bin/python3).

quiz.question: Which of the following is true about CGI scripts?
options: They must be written only in C.
They allow servers to generate dynamic web pages.
They can only serve static content.
quiz.explanation: CGI allows web servers to run programs that produce dynamic content, not just static files.

quiz.question: Where should CGI scripts usually be placed for execution by a web server?
options: The /cgi-bin/ directory or designated CGI-enabled directories
quiz.explanation: Traditionally, CGI scripts are placed in /cgi-bin/ or other directories configured by the web server.
